    DxPower

    The goal of DxPower is to provide functions for power and sample size calculation in confirmatory diagnostic accuracy trials.

    The methodology is based on asymptotic normal approximations and an intersection–union testing framework, where both co-primary endpoints (i.e. sensitivity and specificity) must reject their respective null hypotheses.

    Installation

    The package is available from R-universe:

    install.packages("DxPower", repos = c("https://dcr-unibe-ch.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))

    Alternatively, you can install the development version of DxPower from GitHub with:

    # install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("CTU-Bern/DxPower")

    Current Implementation Status

    The current version implements sample size determination and power evaluation for confirmatory diagnostic accuracy studies with:

    • Binary endpoints (sensitivity and specificity)

    • Single-test designs (superiority against fixed null values) and comparative designs (unpaired and paired, superiority or non-inferiority)

    • Co-primary testing using an intersection–union framework

    • Wald-type (or logit) asymptotic normal approximations, and exact binomial power for the single-test and the unpaired comparative design

    Extensions to continuous endpoints and more general co-primary objectives are planned.

    Statistical Framework

    Study Setting

    We consider a confirmatory diagnostic accuracy study with:

    • Sensitivity SeSe
    • Specificity SpSp
    • Disease prevalence π\pi
    • Total sample size NN

    The number of diseased (cases) and non-diseased (control) subjects is:

    NSe=Nπ,NSp=N(1−π)N_{Se}=N\pi, N_{Sp}=N(1-\pi)

    Diseased and non-diseased subjects form disjoint subgroups. Under standard binomial sampling assumptions, the corresponding estimators of sensitivity and specificity are asymptotically independent.

    Hypotheses

    We consider one-sided superiority hypotheses:

    For sensitivity:

    H0,Se:Se≤Se0vsH1,Se:Se>Se0H_{0,Se}: Se \le Se_0 \quad\text{vs}\quad H_{1,Se}: Se > Se_0

    For specificity:

    H0,Sp:Sp≤Sp0vsH1,Sp:Sp>Sp0H_{0,Sp}: Sp \le Sp_0 \quad\text{vs}\quad H_{1,Sp}: Sp > Sp_0

    Each endpoint is tested at level α=0.025\alpha = 0.025.

    Because both null hypotheses must be rejected to declare overall success, an intersection–union test (IUT) framework is used. Under the global null hypothesis the overall Type I error rate is controlled at level α\alpha without multiplicity adjustment.

    Test Statistic and Approximation

    Both endpoints are evaluated using a Wald-type normal approximation. Under large-sample theory:

    Sê∼N(Se,Se(1−Se)NSe),Sp̂∼N(Sp,Sp(1−Sp)NSp)\hat{Se} \sim N\left( Se,\; \frac{Se(1-Se)}{N_{Se}} \right),\hat{Sp} \sim N\left( Sp,\; \frac{Sp(1-Sp)}{N_{Sp}} \right)

    The sample size formula uses the classical normal approximation with:

    • Variance under the null: Var(Se0)=Se0(1−Se0),Var(Sp0)=Sp0(1−Sp0)Var(Se_0)=Se_0(1-Se_0), Var(Sp_0)=Sp_0(1-Sp_0)
    • Variance under the alternative: Var(Se1)=Se1(1−Se1),Var(Sp1)=Sp1(1−Sp1)Var(Se_1)=Se_1(1-Se_1), Var(Sp_1)=Sp_1(1-Sp_1)

    Overall Power Definition

    Because both endpoints must reject the null hypothesis, an intersection–union test (IUT) is applied.

    Assuming asymptotic independence:

    PowerSe×PowerSp=PoweroverallPower_{Se} \times Power_{Sp}=Power_{overall}

    (1−βSe)×(1−βSp)=(1−βOverall)(1-\beta_{Se}) \times (1-\beta_{Sp})=(1-\beta_{Overall})

    Individual endpoint powers are therefore typically larger than the target overall power.

    Functions

    Overview

    Function Purpose
    power.copr.test() Sample size (power given) or power (N given), single-test design
    power.copr.comp.test() Sample size or power, comparative unpaired or paired design
    ss.copr.conv() Conventional per-endpoint sample size, single-test design
    power.copr.emp() Monte Carlo power, single-test design
    power.copr.comp.emp() Monte Carlo power, unpaired comparative design

    All sample size and power functions return an object of class power.htest.

    Sample size calculation

    power.copr.test(power = ...) computes the required total sample size for a desired overall power and true prevalence π\pi in a confirmatory diagnostic accuracy study with co-primary endpoints.

    Sample Size Formula

    For sensitivity:

    NSe=(z1−αSe0(1−Se0)+z1−βSeSe1(1−Se1))2π×(Se1−Se0)2N_{Se} = \frac{\left( z_{1-\alpha} \sqrt{Se_0(1-Se_0)} + z_{1-\beta_{Se}} \sqrt{Se_1(1-Se_1)} \right)^2} {\pi \times (Se_1 - Se_0)^2}

    For specificity:

    NSp=(z1−αSp0(1−Sp0)+z1−βSpSp1(1−Sp1))2(1−π)×(Sp1−Sp0)2N_{Sp} = \frac{\left( z_{1-\alpha} \sqrt{Sp_0(1-Sp_0)} + z_{1-\beta_{Sp}} \sqrt{Sp_1(1-Sp_1)} \right)^2} {(1-\pi) \times (Sp_1 - Sp_0)^2}

    where:

    • z1−αz_{1-\alpha} is the one-sided critical value
    • z1−βz_{1-\beta} corresponds to the endpoint-specific power
    • Se0,Sp0Se_0, Sp_0 are null values
    • Se1,Sp1Se_1, Sp_1 are alternative values
    • π\pi is the prevalence; determines the allocation of diseased and non-diseased subjects.

    Root-Finding Condition

    The study must satisfy two conditions simultaneously:

    1. The overall power constraint

    (1−βSe)×(1−βSp)=(1−βOverall)(1-\beta_{Se}) \times (1-\beta_{Sp})=(1-\beta_{Overall})

    1. Equal total sample size requirement NSe=NSpN_{Se} = N_{Sp}

    Since the two endpoint-specific powers are linked through the overall power constraint, only one free parameter remains (e.g.,βSe\beta_{Se}).

    βSe=1−1−βOverall1−βSp\beta_{Se} = 1- \frac{1-\beta_{Overall}}{1-\beta_{Sp}}

    The algorithm therefore:

    • Express βSp\beta_{Sp} as a function of βSe\beta_{Se}
    • Substitutes into the two sample size formulas
    • Numerically solves for the value of βSe\beta_{Se} such that

    NSe(βSe)=NSp(βSp)N_{Se}(\beta_{Se}) = N_{Sp}(\beta_{Sp})

    This ensures that:

    • Both endpoints require the same total sample size
    • The overall power equals the desired target
    • The study is optimally balanced

    The resulting total sample size is Ntotal=NSe+NSpN_{total} = N_{Se} + N_{Sp} with allocation driven by prevalence.

    Power calculation

    power.copr.test(N = ...) computes the achieved overall power for a fixed total sample size and true prevalence π\pi in a confirmatory diagnostic accuracy study with co-primary endpoints.

    Endpoint - Specific Power Formula

    Given total NN and true prevalence π\pi:

    NSe=Ntotal⋅πandNSp=Ntotal⋅(1−π)N_{Se} = N_{total} \cdot \pi \quad\text{and}\quad N_{Sp} = N_{total} \cdot (1 - \pi)

    For sensitivity:

    zβSe=NSe|Se1−Se0|−z1−αSe0(1−Se0)Se1(1−Se1)z_{\beta_{Se}} = \frac{\sqrt{N_{Se}}|Se_1 - Se_0| - z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{Se_0(1-Se_0)}}{\sqrt{Se_1(1-Se_1)}}

    PowerSe=Φ(zβSe)Power_{Se} = \Phi(z_{\beta_{Se}})

    Similar for Specificity:

    zβSp=NSp|Sp1−Sp0|−z1−αSp0(1−Sp0)Sp1(1−Sp1)z_{\beta_{Sp}} = \frac{\sqrt{N_{Sp}}|Sp_1 - Sp_0| - z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{Sp_0(1-Sp_0)}}{\sqrt{Sp_1(1-Sp_1)}}

    PowerSp=Φ(zβSp)Power_{Sp} = \Phi(z_{\beta_{Sp}})

    The resulting overall power is

    Poweroverall=PowerSe×PowerSpPower_{overall} = Power_{Se} \times Power_{Sp}

    Remark
    Sample size determination and power evaluation rely on the same asymptotic normal approximation framework, ensuring mathematical consistency. With exact = TRUE the power is the exact binomial rejection probability instead. It is a sawtooth function of NN, so the sample size is found by a scan over integer NN and exact_rule selects either the smallest NN reaching the target ("first") or the smallest NN from which the power stays at or above the target ("stays_above").

    Comparative designs

    power.copr.comp.test() handles studies comparing an experimental test with a comparator, for sensitivity and specificity, with superiority or non-inferiority hypotheses (type.se, type.sp, margins delta.se, delta.sp).

    • design = "unpaired": subjects are randomised to one of the two tests. The variance under the null is set by variance ("null", "pooled" or "unpooled").
    • design = "paired": all subjects receive both tests. The discordance probabilities psi.d and psi.nd must be given. Superiority uses the Miettinen formula and non-inferiority the Liu score method.

    The significance level alpha is one-sided (default 0.025) as for the single-test design. The overall power is again the product of the two endpoint powers.

    Conventional sample size

    ss.copr.conv() implements the conventional three-step approach of Stark et al. (2022). It calculates the number of diseased subjects needed for the sensitivity and the number of non-diseased subjects needed for the specificity, each with its own endpoint power. These are divided by the prevalence and by one minus the prevalence, and the maximum is taken. The endpoint with the smaller requirement is overpowered, so the overall power is typically above the target.

    Empirical (simulated) power

    power.copr.emp() and power.copr.comp.emp() give vectorised Monte Carlo estimates of the overall power for the single-test and the unpaired comparative design. They are used to check the analytic results and are not interchangeable, because the comparator is estimated in the unpaired design.

    Example

    Required Sample Size 

    
res <- power.copr.test(
  power = 0.80,
  prev = 0.5,
  se.e = 0.85, se.min = 0.70,
  sp.e = 0.85, sp.min = 0.65,
  alpha = 0.025
)

res
#> 
#>      Single-test design (sample size calculation)
#>               Wald normal approximation 
#> 
#>               n = 134
#>           n_dis = 67
#>        n_nondis = 67
#>            prev = 0.5
#>       sig.level = 0.025
#>     alternative = one.sided
#>           power = 0.8018057
#>        power_se = 0.8220385
#>        power_sp = 0.9753871
#>       ci_method = wald
#>           exact = FALSE
#>    target_power = 0.8
#> 
#> NOTE: n is the total sample size.

    Achieved Power for Fixed Sample Size 

    
pow <- power.copr.test(
  N = res$n,
  prev = 0.5,
  se.e = 0.85, se.min = 0.70,
  sp.e = 0.85, sp.min = 0.65,
  alpha = 0.025
)
pow
#> 
#>      Single-test design (power calculation)
#>            Wald normal approximation 
#> 
#>               n = 134
#>           n_dis = 67
#>        n_nondis = 67
#>            prev = 0.5
#>       sig.level = 0.025
#>     alternative = one.sided
#>           power = 0.8018057
#>        power_se = 0.8220385
#>        power_sp = 0.9753871
#>       ci_method = wald
#>           exact = FALSE
#> 
#> NOTE: n is the total sample size.

  power = 0.80,
  prev = 0.6,
  se.c = 0.75, se.e = 0.85,

)
